To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the sleep of students is not as good as it could be and that there is a clear link between sleep quality and daytime alertness.

almost half of the students in our study were at risk of not obtaining enough sleep; almost a quarter of students were averaging six hours or fewer per night; the majority of students had poor sleep habits, which was reflected in their daytime alertness; students with better sleep habits were more likely to have a permanent, personal sleep space; and finally that the students' perception of their own sleep quality and their academic performance were strongly related to their daytime alertness.

almost one in every two students were averaging less than the recommended number of sleep hours per night; towards one in every five were averaging six or less; and, the quality of sleep and the resulting levels and quality of daytime alertness was clearly linked to having an adequate personal space for sleep.
